column2: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) v2026.09
column7: - Many moderation and filtering controls inspect mainly the text channel, so a payload hidden in an image, audio, video, or file metadata can still steer a multimodal model unnoticed. · - Self-hosted AI runtimes listen on predictable ports and standard API paths, so attackers find model-serving hosts by scanning or by querying scan services such as Shodan and Censys. · - Agent and SaaS platforms host agents behind URL patterns built from tenant, environment, or agent names, and default configurations keep those patterns the same across victims. · - Most major AI assistants accept a prefilled prompt through a URL parameter such as ?q= or ?prompt=, so whoever controls a link can write the first turn of a user's conversation. · - Attackers who reach a working agent can map its tools, parameters, permissions, and embedded credentials at runtime by testing requests, without reading its configuration. · - Indirect prompt injection arrives through documents, email, databases, or websites the agent ingests, and the hijacked agent acts with whatever privileges the AI system holds. · - Legitimate businesses also poison assistants: Microsoft found more than 50 memory manipulation prompts from 31 companies in about 60 days of email traffic, several aimed at health and finance.
column8: - Any agent whose context takes in untrusted data can have its tools invoked by prompt injections in that data, with confidentiality, integrity, or availability violations as the result. · - Production models require users to verify identity, API endpoints require authentication, and operators monitor model queries against usage policy. · - Validation of inputs and outputs for agent tools and data sources runs outside the AI agent, covering schema checks, leakage checks, and removal of injections or unsafe code. · - A human decision maker gives final approval of agent actions; audit agents may assist the review but do not replace the human approver. · - Agent execution environments start from a clean base image on each run and carry forward no operational state. · - Defenders verify the cryptographic checksum of every AI artifact to confirm an attacker did not modify the file. · - Any interaction with a decoy AI service, agent, or credential signals unauthorized activity with high confidence, because authorized users and workflows have no reason to touch it.
column9: - Deception with AI honeypots: the security team places monitored decoy AI services, agents, and credentials beside real assets and feeds captured prompts and tooling into detection rules. · - Least privilege: the deploying team grants a privileged or multi-user agent only the tools and resources its designated task requires, enforced with RBAC or ABAC. · - Delegated access: the platform team gives each tool shared across agents the permissions, identity, and limits of the calling agent, set in the MCP server or tool configuration. · - Consequence-scaled confirmation: once untrusted data enters an LLM's context, the system blocks automatic tool calls or asks the user to confirm, and always asks for high-consequence actions. · - Staged guardrails: developers check prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, and outputs at each workflow stage, log each guardrail decision, and add observed failures to evaluation datasets. · - Agent telemetry: operators log model inputs and outputs and, for agents, intermediate steps, data access, tool use, install commands, and the agent's identity. · - Threat-informed red teaming: an AI red team runs recurring authorized exercises against models, data, agent memory and tools, and data flows before deployment and during operation.
